title: Breath as an offering
hook: in the middle of a list of offerings, the Gita slips in the breath itself
carry: even breath can be yajna, an offering
tomorrow: How do you tame a lion of a breath?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patanjali's eight limbs: the yamas and niyamas, the seat, then the breath. Yoga begins with the yamas, not the breath.
screen: `THE EIGHT LIMBS.` · `YOGA BEGINS WITH THE YAMAS.`

segments.voice: Two armies wait on the field of Kurukshetra, and in chapter four of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna, driving Arjuna's chariot, is making a list. Some offer their sacrifice in fire. Some offer their wealth, some study, some strict vows. It reads like a tour of the ways a person can give something up. Then, tucked into the list, a line that sounds almost like a breathing class. Some offer the in-breath into the out-breath, and the out-breath into the in-breath. No altar, no grain, no butter poured on flames. Just the breath, handed back and forth.
screen: `THE GITA MAKES A LIST.` → `FIRE, WEALTH, STUDY, VOWS.` → `AND THEN: THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: The verse, chapter four, twenty-nine, in paraphrase: some offer the in-breath into the out-breath, and the out-breath into the in-breath, checking the movement of both, devoted to the regulation of breath. That last phrase is pranayama, right there in the Sanskrit. To hear how bold that is, remember what yajna, sacrifice, meant: the Vedic fire rite, grain and ghee poured into Agni, the fire, with chanted verses. Hindus still do it, around a wedding's sacred fire or a havan for a new home. Krishna keeps the fire and widens it. Around this verse he lists offerings with no fire at all: study, vows, the senses held back. A few verses later he says sacrifice made of knowledge is greater than sacrifice made of things. So the breath on this list isn't a warm-up before the real offering. It is one. That's one of the Gita's big teachings: a whole life can be yajna, offered, not only the moments at the altar. Notice the shape, too. It's already a sequence, the simplest there is. Each half is an offering into the other. The out-breath isn't an ending; it's what the in-breath is given to. Commentators read the verse in different ways. Some take it as a technical note on the in-breath, the out-breath and the hold between. Others read it more widely, as one more inner offering in a chapter full of them. The text leaves room for both. What it does settle is that the breath belongs on the list.
screen: `IN-BREATH OFFERED INTO OUT-BREATH.` · `YAJNA: THE FIRE RITE, WIDENED.` · `STUDY, VOWS, THE BREATH ITSELF.` · then, large: `A WHOLE LIFE CAN BE OFFERED.`

segments.voice: For a few breaths, change nothing; notice where the out-breath ends, and let the next in-breath receive what the last one let go. Then watch the two turning points, out becoming in and in becoming out, without lengthening or holding anything, and after a handful of rounds let the breath carry on by itself. If you pray, you can hold the Gita's picture lightly in mind: breath given into breath.
Pranayama sequences. Breath practices set in an order. Today, the Gita's picture of one: in-breath offered into out-breath, and back.
Your line: even breath can be yajna, an offering. Each half is given to the other, and nothing is thrown away. Go gently.

howItsDone: Some Hindus who practice pranayama understand it, with Gita 4.29, as an offering in itself; yajna also goes on as the fire rite at weddings and home havans, and many families offer food to God before eating it as prasad.
